steps.say: Non muscle invasive bladder cancer stays above the bladder muscle, which is why it can be shaved off from inside rather than removing the whole bladder. It comes in three stages that every trainee recites: Ta is a fluffy papillary frond floating above the lining, T1 has invaded the lamina propria just beneath, and Tis, also grouped as Tis / CIS, is a flat red high grade patch that looks innocent but behaves badly.
steps.tx: **NMIBC** (bladder cancer sparing the muscle, non-muscle invasive bladder cancer) spans **Ta** (non-invasive papillary fronds), **T1** (invasion of lamina propria, the subepithelial connective tissue), and **Tis** (carcinoma in situ, flat high grade disease, grouped Tis / CIS). Ta floats above the lining, T1 nibbles the tissue beneath it, and Tis spreads flat and angry, so the stage at first sight already forecasts recurrence risk and follow up intensity.

vis.alt: Diagram of urothelial carcinoma sites and types across the bladder wall layers.
vis.caption: Urothelial carcinoma sites and types: Ta, T1, and Tis mapped on bladder wall layers. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The first operation is both diagnosis and treatment: transurethral resection shaves the tumour off through a scope passed up the urethra, with no cut on the belly. But a shallow shave is a staging disaster, because without bladder muscle in the specimen the pathologist cannot tell T1 from deeper invasion. Every adequate resection must therefore bite deep enough to include detrusor muscle in the jar.
steps.tx: Perform **TURBT** (scope resection through the urethra, transurethral resection of bladder tumour) by shaving the lesion in layers until the specimen holds **detrusor muscle** (bladder wall muscle, **muscularis propria**). Without muscle the pathologist cannot separate T1 from muscle invasion, and the patient is understaged and undertreated. Record muscle presence in every report: its absence automatically triggers a second look operation within weeks.

vis.alt: Cystoscopic view of a bladder tumour as seen during transurethral resection.
vis.caption: Bladder tumour at cystoscopy: resect deep enough to include detrusor muscle. Credit: image bank.

steps.say: Even a good first resection misses tumour more often than surgeons admit, especially flat carcinoma in situ hiding at the edges. So every T1 cancer, every high grade cancer, and every resection that arrived without muscle earns a planned second look. This restaging TURBT goes back within two to six weeks to resect the scar base, and it upstages one patient in three while clearing residual tumour in the rest.
steps.tx: Book a **restaging TURBT** (planned second-look resection, **second-look TURBT**) within **2 to 6 weeks** (two to six weeks) for all **T1 tumours** (lamina invading cancers), high-grade tumours, or resections **lacking detrusor muscle** (no muscle in the jar). The second pass resects the scar base, finds residual tumour in half the cases, and upstages muscle invasion that changes the whole plan from bladder sparing to bladder removal.

rows: T1, high grade, or no muscle
Restaging TURBT of the scar base

steps.say: Fresh resection leaves floating cancer cells that seed new tumours within hours, so one immediate wash of chemotherapy locks in the gain. A single postoperative instillation of mitomycin C at 40 milligrams, or gemcitabine as the modern alternative, given into the bladder within 24 hours of TURBT, cuts recurrence by 35 percent in low to intermediate risk disease. It is cheap, quick, and skipped far too often.
steps.tx: Give a single **immediate instillation** (bladder wash within a day of surgery) of intravesical chemotherapy, **mitomycin C 40 mg** (forty milligrams) or gemcitabine, **within 24 hours** (one day) of TURBT. This one wash destroys floating cells and cuts recurrence by **35%** (thirty five in a hundred) in low-to-intermediate risk disease. Hold the dose only for bladder perforation or heavy bleeding, because the benefit evaporates if the wash is delayed.

steps.say: High risk disease needs the living vaccine, not just chemicals. BCG induction delivers a weekly bladder instillation for six straight weeks, provoking an immune storm inside the bladder wall. Then comes the long haul: the SWOG maintenance protocol gives three weekly booster instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 36 months, stretching protection across three full years.
steps.tx: Treat high-risk NMIBC with **BCG induction** (weekly live vaccine washes for **6 weeks**, Bacillus Calmette-Guerin provoking bladder wall immunity) followed by **3-year maintenance** (booster years) per the **SWOG protocol** (three weekly instillations at **3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 months**). Induction ignites the immune attack and maintenance keeps it burning, because stopping early lets high grade disease roar back within the year.

rows: Early stop invites high grade return

steps.say: BCG is safe in the bladder but lethal in the bloodstream, so every instillation team must know the sepsis drill. Fever with crashing blood pressure after BCG means disseminated infection, and it is a medical emergency, not a flu to watch overnight. Stop all further BCG at once and start full antitubercular therapy with isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol plus high dose corticosteroids, exactly as for tuberculosis.
steps.tx: Treat **BCG sepsis** (disseminated vaccine infection) as an emergency: fever with **hemodynamic instability** (crashing blood pressure) after instillation needs instant BCG cessation plus **antitubercular therapy** (tuberculosis medicines: **isoniazid**, **rifampin**, **ethambutol**) with high-dose **corticosteroids** (rescue steroids). Never rechallenge with BCG after sepsis, because the next dose can kill, and never dismiss post BCG fever with hypotension as a routine reaction.

steps.say: Some cancers shrug off the vaccine, and naming that failure precisely matters because it opens the cystectomy door. BCG unresponsive disease means high grade Ta or T1 persisting within six months, or carcinoma in situ lingering within twelve months, despite adequate BCG. For these patients the bladder has voted against itself, and radical cystectomy, complete bladder removal with urinary diversion, becomes the standard advice.
steps.tx: Label **BCG-unresponsive** (vaccine beaten disease) when high-grade Ta or T1 recurs **within 6 months** (six months) or CIS persists **within 12 months** (twelve months) of adequate BCG. The standard counsel is **radical cystectomy** (complete bladder removal with urinary diversion), because persistent high grade disease invades muscle while doctors dither. Reserve bladder sparing only for patients unfit for surgery or refusing it after frank risk disclosure.

points: Ta T1 back in 6 months, CIS in 12
right.title: BCG-unresponsive

steps.say: For patients who cannot or will not lose the bladder, two approved lifelines now preserve it. Pembrolizumab, an anti PD-1 checkpoint immunotherapy given by vein, and nadofaragene firadenovec, a gene therapy vector dripped into the bladder that makes the lining secrete interferon, are both cleared for BCG unresponsive carcinoma in situ. Neither matches cystectomy for cure, but both buy selected patients extra years with their own bladder.
steps.tx: Offer **pembrolizumab** (vein given anti-PD-1 checkpoint drug) and **nadofaragene firadenovec** (bladder dripped adenoviral vector gene therapy) as bladder-preserving options for **BCG-unresponsive CIS** (vaccine beaten flat disease) in cystectomy-ineligible patients. Both are FDA-approved for this niche, with complete response rates that spare selected bladders for years. Frame them honestly: cystectomy still cures most, while these lifelines suit the unfit or the refusers.
